solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Bank payment system taken up by non-union worker?

indicators.note: in a down clue, taking something up means reading it from the bottom, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: BACS is the UK interbank automated payment system (Bankers' Automated Clearing Services)

explanation.surface: A query about whether a strikebreaker would sign up to the banks' automated payment scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken up' turns BACS round. BACS is the British system that moves salaries and direct debits between banks.
explanation.definitionFit: Strikebreaker slang: someone who works on while union members strike, or refuses to join, is called a scab.

clue.text: One assaulting you verbally, getting stuck into six-pack, about to get comeuppance

indicators.note: being stuck into something means being lodged inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a six-pack is a set of well-defined abdominal muscles, ABS

indicators.note: verbally signals that the word is spoken, and the letter U is pronounced like the word you

parts.note: the word you, said out loud, is the letter U

indicators.note: in a down clue, a come-up turns the word upward, so it reads backwards

parts.note: RE means about or concerning, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: Someone shouting insults at a gym-toned person who is about to get what's coming to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting stuck into' and 'comeuppance' (an upward turn in a down clue) do the work. 'One assaulting you verbally' reads as the whole definition, but 'you verbally' is the letter U, and a six-pack is toned stomach muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: An abuser is a person who attacks or mistreats another, physically or with insults.

clue.text: A phonebox I vandalised, being unable to connect with abroad?

definitions.text: being unable to connect with abroad?

indicators.note: something vandalised is smashed up, so its letters are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: A wrecked phone box means you can't call anyone overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vandalised' shuffles the ten letters of A PHONEBOX I. The surface pictures a broken phone line to foreign countries; the definition means a dislike of foreigners.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenophobia is fear or hatred of foreigners, a playful 'inability to connect' with people from other countries.

clue.text: A guy getting date with a girl

parts.note: guy is an informal word for a man

explanation.surface: A man lines up a date with a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's guy and girl are both just pieces: the girl is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Amanda is a female given name, and crosswords freely define such names as a girl.

clue.text: American comes up with crushed garlic for medical use

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the piece is read from the bottom, backwards

parts.note: US is short for American, as in the United States

indicators.note: garlic that is crushed is pulped, so its letters are mashed into a new order

explanation.surface: An American recommends crushed garlic as a home remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes up' is a turnaround because this is a down clue, and 'crushed' is the anagram signal; the surface makes both sound like cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgical describes things used in or relating to surgery, so a surgical item is meant for medical use.

clue.text: Stitched up all the points

parts.note: the four points of the compass are South, East, West and North, abbreviated S, E, W, N
East, one of the four compass points, is E
West, one of the four compass points, is W
North, one of the four compass points, is N

explanation.surface: Someone framed on every count, every point in the case against them.
explanation.walkthrough: All four compass points are used, one letter each, arranged to make the word. 'Stitched up' suggests a frame-up, but here it simply means sewn.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stitched together with needle and thread has been sewn, the past participle of the verb sew.

clue.text: Make extended agreement about rights surrounding antique books

indicators.note: about here means going round the outside, so the agreement encloses what follows

parts.note: a pact is an agreement

indicators.note: the rights are placed either side of the books, so they enclose them

parts.note: R is an abbreviation for right, so two of them, rights, give RR
the Old Testament, OT, is the ancient set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A deal is lengthened, covering rights to some old books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounding' and 'about' are both containers, nested. Antique books are the Old Testament, the older half of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: To protract something is to prolong it or draw it out in time, which is making it extended.

clue.text: Railway Tavern acquiring around 60 per cent of World's End? Not likely

indicators.note: the first part acquires the second by having the trimmed word placed around it, so one sits within the other
only the opening six of the ten letters of the word are kept, sixty per cent of it

parts.note: the Apocalypse is the end of the world described in Revelation
PH is short for public house, as marked on maps, and a tavern is a pub

explanation.surface: A pub called the Railway Tavern buying most of a rival named the World's End seems far-fetched.
explanation.walkthrough: '60 per cent of' cuts APOCALYPSE to APOCAL; 'acquiring around' sets RYPH inside it. Railway Tavern and World's End read as pub names.
explanation.definitionFit: An apocryphal story is of doubtful truth, widely told but probably invented, so it is not likely to be true.

clue.text: Politician appearing in Telegraph as opposed to satellite TV?

definitions.meaning: Vince ..., then Business Secretary, appeared in the Daily Telegraph in December 2010 when its undercover reporters recorded him boasting of declaring war on Rupert Murdoch
television delivered through underground wires rather than from a satellite dish

explanation.surface: A topical reference to a minister caught by this newspaper's reporters and his clash with a satellite broadcaster.
explanation.walkthrough: Murdoch's Sky is satellite television; the other way to receive pay TV is by wire. Telegraph can also mean a wired message, a further echo of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The politician's surname is also the name for wired television delivered through ducts, the alternative to a dish.

clue.text: E.g. Cheshire route maps redrafted

indicators.note: something redrafted is written out again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Road maps of the county of Cheshire have been redrawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'redrafted' rearranges ROUTE MAPS. 'Cheshire' looks like the English county but is the cheese; mousetrap is slang for cheap, ordinary cheese like Cheshire or Cheddar.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousetrap is British slang for plain, inexpensive hard cheese of the sort used to bait traps, and Cheshire is one such cheese.

clue.text: Graduate's very good on instrument

parts.note: a BA is a Bachelor of Arts graduate, and the possessive adds S
so means very, as in so tired
on can mean acceptable or feasible, as in that's not on, so good

explanation.surface: A graduate is a very good player of a musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface praises a student's playing, but every word before 'instrument' is a building piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The bassoon is a low-pitched double-reed woodwind instrument of the orchestra.

clue.text: Give example of negative comeback from inheritance

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the pieces are read in the reverse direction

parts.note: to cite something is to quote it as an example

explanation.surface: Someone illustrating a downside of a legacy, in a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comeback' turns CITENEG round.
explanation.definitionFit: Genetic traits are passed down by heredity, so they come from inheritance in the biological sense.

clue.text: Hagar the Horrible's cry

indicators.note: horrible here means messed up or mangled, so the name's letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: The war cry of Hagar the Horrible, the cartoon Viking.
explanation.walkthrough: Hagar the Horrible is a comic strip Viking; 'the Horrible's' rearranges HAGAR. The surface reads the name as a whole, but only the first word is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: This interjection is an exclamation of frustration, horror or anger, the kind of shout written in comics.

clue.text: Club's lost villa, island structure blown away

indicators.note: a club that has lost part of its name drops those letters

parts.note: Aston Villa is a Birmingham football club, its name in two words
the second word of the Birmingham club's name
the word villa is the part of the club's name that goes
a shed is a simple building or structure

explanation.surface: A football club's villa and island building were destroyed by a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: ASTON VILLA is an English Premier League football club in Birmingham; 'lost villa' leaves ASTON. 'Blown away' sounds like storm damage but means amazed.
explanation.definitionFit: Blown away is an idiom for being amazed or greatly impressed, the same as stunned by surprise.

clue.text: Escort to affirm?

definitions.meaning: to escort someone is to go along with them
read as to a firm, a firm is a business; stammered, a business becomes a c-company

explanation.surface: An escort agency asked to confirm a booking.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is whimsical: 'affirm' split as 'a firm', a business, said with a stutter on its first letter. The question mark flags the liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: To go with someone as a companion or escort is to keep them company; a firm is likewise a business or company.

clue.text: Masked man running around Europe to put things right

indicators.note: running around suggests moving every which way, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A masked vigilante dashes about the continent setting wrongs right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running around' rearranges MASKED MAN with E.
explanation.definitionFit: To make amends is to compensate for a wrong done, an idiom for putting things right.

clue.text: Tom fixes boat, but that's not the big picture

parts.note: Tom Thumb is the tiny hero of the English fairy tale, so Tom suggests his surname
to nail is to fix with nails, so nails means fixes
a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat

explanation.surface: Tom repairs a boat, though that is only part of the story.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Thumb is a thumb-sized boy in English folklore. 'that's not the big picture' is literal: a small, quick drawing.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief, rough outline or small drawing, lacking detail, is by its nature not the big picture.

clue.text: Like Grease, not censored but with ending revised, so released with 'U'

indicators.note: only the closing pair of letters is changed round, so the end is turned back while the start stays

parts.note: a film that is uncut has had nothing removed by censors

indicators.note: letters released are set free to fall into a new order

explanation.surface: The film Grease, given a new ending, is let out on a U certificate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with ending revised' swaps UNCUT's last two letters to give UNCTU; 'released' rearranges SO and U to OUS. U is the British film rating for all ages; Grease is the musical, but 'Grease' means grease.
explanation.definitionFit: Unctuous literally means oily or greasy, so it describes something like grease.

clue.text: Unchanging, heartless Irish fool — that's my opinion

parts.note: as is means in the present condition, without any change

indicators.note: a heartless word loses its central letter

parts.note: eejit is the Irish and Scottish pronunciation-spelling of idiot

explanation.surface: A stubborn, unfeeling Irish idiot giving his opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' takes the middle J out of EEJIT, leaving EEIT. EEJIT is the Irish and Scots colloquial form of idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces a personal view, the same idea as saying this is how I judge the matter.

clue.text: Fruit I put in elaborate entrance

indicators.note: the single letter is put inside the rearranged letters
elaborate means intricately worked, so the letters are reworked into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone placing fruit in a grand doorway as decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'elaborate' rearranges ENTRANCE to NECTARNE; 'put in' places I inside. 'Elaborate' looks like a description of the entrance.
explanation.definitionFit: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned variety of peach, a stone fruit.

clue.text: Range formerly part of camp

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
a tent is one unit of a campsite

explanation.surface: A range that was once part of a military camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' suggests a firing range at an old camp, but it means scope.
explanation.definitionFit: Extent and range both mean the scope or reach over which something applies.

clue.text: A ring of rock

parts.note: to toll is to ring a bell slowly

explanation.surface: A circle of stone, simply described.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring is a bell's toll in the wordplay, while the whole clue describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef or island enclosing a lagoon, so a circle of rock in the sea.

clue.text: Get the better of Oxford fool

parts.note: OU is short for Oxford University
a twit is a silly person, a fool

explanation.surface: Getting the better of an Oxford idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: To outwit is to defeat someone through cleverness, beating them by being smarter.

clue.text: E.g. boerewors?

parts.note: boerewors is a spiced South African farmers' coil of minced meat, and the word itself is South African usage

explanation.surface: Asking what kind of thing boerewors is.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 2,5 the answer gives SA USAGE: the word boerewors is South African usage, which is the hidden joke of the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Boerewors is a coarse beef-and-pork link, so it is an example of this cased meat product.

clue.text: Surrounded in about 1001 AD

indicators.note: one piece goes in and the other is about it, wrapping it

parts.note: in Roman numerals M is 1000 and I is 1, giving MI

explanation.surface: A historical event, enclosed in around the year 1001.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in about' is the container signal; 1001 is written in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Amid means in the middle of or encircled by, so it carries the sense of being surrounded by.

clue.text: Piece of hi-fi equipment was first used in rock

indicators.note: the letter is used inside the other word, so it is placed within it

parts.note: to teeter is to rock or wobble unsteadily

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of was is used

explanation.surface: A hi-fi part was first used in rock music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock' looks like the music the hi-fi plays, but it means wobble.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweeter is a small loudspeaker unit in a hi-fi that reproduces high-frequency sound.

clue.text: Echo of lift shafts

indicators.note: an echo repeats a sound, so the word comes as it is heard

parts.note: to lift something is to raise it

explanation.surface: The sound of a lift echoing in its shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Echo of' gives a word that is heard like RAISE. 'lift shafts' reads as one phrase; the shafts are beams of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Shafts of light are beams, and beams of light are also called rays.

clue.text: One outwardly inured to eccentric scholarship

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit on the outside, with the single letter enclosed
eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters are put in a strange new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A person who has grown hardened to an oddball's academic learning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' rearranges INURED TO to ERUDTION, and 'outwardly' has that around I.
explanation.definitionFit: Erudition is deep, wide learning acquired by study, the same as scholarship in its sense of knowledge.

clue.text: Day 17: there's something fancy on the table

parts.note: the answer to 17 down means greasy, a synonym of slick and oily

explanation.surface: A diary entry: on day 17, something decorative is laid on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: '17' points to the answer of 17 Down, whose meaning gives OILY. A doily is a decorative lace mat.
explanation.definitionFit: A doily is an ornamental lace or paper mat put under cakes or dishes, a fancy item for the table.
